title: Thermodynamics and Energy Systems
description: How energy moves through engines, power stations, refrigerators and walls, and what limits it. Each lesson practises one engineering judgement: choosing a system, reading a state, testing an efficiency claim, improving a cycle, sizing insulation or checking a power figure.
audience: Adults who know specific heat, the ideal gas law, the first law and Carnot efficiency in outline from the Physics II course, and want to work with energy balances, tables and cycles as an engineer does. Logarithms and exponents are used; calculus is not.
outcomes: You'll be able to draw a boundary round a real device and write its energy balance.
You'll be able to find the state of water from a table and use enthalpy to size a turbine, pump or condenser.
You'll be able to test an efficiency claim against the Carnot limit and say where a real machine loses work.
You'll be able to analyse steam, gas-turbine, piston-engine and combined cycles and say which change would improve each.
You'll be able to judge a heat pump's COP, a wall's insulation and a power station's heat rate against what the physics allows.

lessons.title: Where you draw the boundary
lessons.objective: Choose a system and boundary for a real device, classify it as isolated, closed or open, and list what crosses the boundary as mass, heat or work.

concepts.title: System and boundary
concepts.summary: The matter or region you choose to study; the right boundary depends on what you know and what you are asked.

concepts.title: Isolated, closed and open systems
concepts.summary: Isolated: nothing crosses. Closed: heat and work cross but no mass. Open: mass, heat and work all cross.

concepts.title: Heat and work are energy in transit
concepts.summary: A system holds internal, kinetic and potential energy; heat and work exist only as energy crossing the boundary.

concepts.title: Sign convention
concepts.summary: Count heat into the system and work out of the system as positive, and say so before writing a balance.

misconceptions: A closed system is sealed and insulated. It has no mass crossing, but heat and work still can.
A hot body contains heat. It holds internal energy; heat only exists while energy crosses a boundary because of a temperature difference.
There is one correct boundary. A pump, a turbine or the whole loop can each be the right choice, depending on the question.
Energy is used up in a device. It changes form or leaves across the boundary; the first law balances.
sequence: Open with a steam plant drawn as four boxes and ask what you would need to know to study just the pump.
Define system, surroundings and boundary; classify by what may cross: isolated, closed, open.
Show heat and work as energy in transit using the pump: water in and out (mass), shaft power (work), a warm casing (heat).
State the first law for a boundary and fix the sign convention: heat in, work out.
Move the boundary around the same plant (pump, turbine, whole loop) and list what crosses each time.
Recap as a three-step habit: draw the boundary, label every crossing, choose signs.
examples: Boundary round a feed pump: water crosses at inlet and outlet (open); the shaft does work on the water; the casing loses a little heat. Boundary round boiler, turbine, condenser and pump together: no mass crosses, so the loop is a closed system with heat in at the boiler, heat out at the condenser and net work out.
A turbine's work in the pack's convention: work out is positive, heat leaking through the casing is negative heat (heat in is positive).
The pack's own range of systems: the water on one side of a heat exchanger, the fluid in a length of pipe, or the whole lubricating oil system of a diesel engine.

figures.shows: A four-box steam plant (boiler, turbine, condenser, pump) with three dashed boundaries (pump only, turbine only, whole loop). Arrows for mass, heat and work are drawn for the chosen boundary.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between boundaries and tap each arrow that crosses to label it mass, heat or work.

figures.shows: Three rows (isolated, closed, open) and three columns (mass, heat, work) with the cells blank.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in whether each can cross.

questionPlan.sample: A steam turbine's casing is the boundary. Steam enters and leaves, the shaft turns a generator, and a little heat leaks out through the casing. What type of system is this?
questionPlan.answer: Open, because steam crosses along with work and heat
choices: Closed, because the casing is sealed against leaks
Open, because steam crosses along with work and heat
Isolated, because the casing is insulated against heat loss
questionPlan.why: Isolated means nothing at all crosses. Closed means no mass crosses, but steam does.

questionPlan.sample: A boundary is drawn round the boiler, turbine, condenser and pump together, and the same water circulates round the loop. Which statement about this boundary is right?
questionPlan.answer: Heat and work cross but no mass does, so it is closed
choices: Mass crosses at the boiler and condenser, so it is open
Nothing crosses, since the water never leaves the loop
Heat and work cross but no mass does, so it is closed
questionPlan.why: The water stays inside, so it is closed. Heat and work still cross, so it is not isolated.

questionPlan.sample: A note on a drawing says: 'The steam in this vessel holds 500 Btu of heat and 200 Btu of work.' What is the best correction?
questionPlan.answer: Neither is stored: the steam holds internal energy only
choices: Heat is stored in the steam, and work is stored in the shaft
Neither is stored: the steam holds internal energy only
Both are stored, so the two can be added up
questionPlan.why: A system never possesses heat or work. Only the first correction names why.

questionPlan.sample: With heat into the system and work out of the system counted positive, a feed pump does 6 kW of work on the water. What is the pump's work term?
questionPlan.answer: -6 kW
choices: +6 kW
-6 kW
0 kW
questionPlan.why: The pump puts work into the fluid, which is negative work out of it.

questionPlan.sample: Boundary round a feed pump. Sort each item as mass, heat, work, or does not cross: (1) water entering the inlet, (2) shaft power from the motor, (3) warmth escaping from the casing into the room, (4) the rise in the water's pressure, (5) electricity feeding the motor.
questionPlan.answer: Mass: 1. Work: 2. Heat: 3. Does not cross: 4 (a property of the water) and 5 (outside the boundary)
choices: Mass
Heat
Work
Does not cross
questionPlan.why: Energy that is neither mass flow nor shaft work is heat.

lessons.title: Which state is this?
lessons.objective: Place water in the right region from its temperature and pressure, read enthalpy from a saturation table or from quality, and judge whether an ideal gas model is safe.

concepts.title: Saturation
concepts.summary: At a given pressure, liquid and vapour can coexist only at one temperature; the table pairs each saturation temperature with its pressure.

concepts.title: Compressed liquid, mixture, superheated vapour
concepts.summary: Below the saturation temperature at that pressure the water is liquid; at it, a mixture; above it, superheated vapour.

concepts.title: Quality
concepts.summary: Mass of vapour over total mass in the mixture region; h = hf + x hfg.

concepts.title: When the ideal gas model holds
concepts.summary: Pv = RT with absolute temperature and pressure suits gases well above their boiling point at modest pressure, and fails near saturation and at very high pressure (water's critical point is 22.1 MPa).

misconceptions: Water at 100 C is steam. At 101 kPa it can be liquid, mixture or vapour; the region depends on pressure as well.
Temperature and pressure fix the state everywhere. In the mixture region they are tied together, so a third property such as quality is needed.
Quality is the liquid fraction. It is the vapour fraction; the liquid fraction is moisture, 1 - x.
Gauge pressure and Celsius can go into Pv = RT. Both must be absolute.
Steam behaves like air. The pack gives gamma 1.324 for steam at 100 C against 1.4 for air.
sequence: Heat water at constant pressure: temperature rises, stops during boiling, rises again. Name the three regions.
Read the SI saturation table: each row pairs T with the saturation pressure, hf and hfg; hg is hf + hfg.
Decide the region by comparing the given pressure with the saturation pressure at the given temperature.
Use quality: h = hf + x hfg, and run it backwards to find x from h.
Note that liquid water is nearly incompressible: its density changes by only about 6% from 15 to 15,000 psia.
Decide when Pv = RT is safe: absolute scales, the 5% rule for a sealed gas, and when not to use it.
examples: Water at 200 C and 1,000 kPa. The table gives 1,554.3 kPa at 200 C and 1,002.7 kPa at 180 C. At 1,000 kPa water boils just under 180 C, so 200 C is above it: superheated vapour.
The handbook's case: steam at 400 psia and quality 90%, h = 424.2 + 0.90 x 780.4 = 1,126.56 Btu/lbm.
A sealed rigid cylinder of air reads 30 psig at 70 F; atmosphere 14.7 psia. Heated to 190 F: P = 44.7 x 650/530 = 54.8 psia = 40.1 psig.

figures.shows: Saturation rows from 100 C to 200 C: T, P, hf, hfg, with hg left for the learner to add.
figures.learnerAction: Compute hg = hf + hfg for chosen rows.

figures.shows: Temperature against specific enthalpy for water heated at constant pressure: a rising line, a flat line, a rising line, with region names hidden.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a state marker along the line and name the region it is in.
figures.placement: Regions and the flat boiling line

questionPlan.sample: The table gives a saturation pressure of 1,554.3 kPa at 200 C and 1,002.7 kPa at 180 C. Water at 200 C is held at 1,000 kPa. Which region is it in?
questionPlan.answer: Superheated vapour
choices: Superheated vapour
Compressed (subcooled) liquid
Saturated liquid-vapour mixture
questionPlan.why: At 1,000 kPa water boils just under 180 C. Compressed liquid would need pressure above 1,554.3 kPa at 200 C.

questionPlan.sample: Wet steam at 200 C has h = 2,400 kJ/kg. The table gives hf = 851.9 and hfg = 1,937.3 kJ/kg. What is its quality?
questionPlan.why: x = (h - hf) / hfg.

questionPlan.sample: Wet steam in a condenser is at 100 C. What else must you know to fix its state?
questionPlan.answer: Its quality, because 100 C already fixes the pressure
choices: Its quality, because 100 C already fixes the pressure
Its pressure, because 100 C only fixes the temperature
Nothing more, since 100 C fixes the state of water
questionPlan.why: In the mixture region T and P are tied, so a third property such as quality is needed.

questionPlan.sample: A sealed rigid cylinder of air reads 30 psig at 70 F. The atmosphere is 14.7 psia. It is heated to 190 F. What does the gauge read? (R = F + 460.)
questionPlan.answer: 40.1 psig (accept 39.5 to 40.5)
questionPlan.why: Convert both to absolute, scale by the temperature ratio, convert back. Scaling the gauge value directly gives a wrong answer.

questionPlan.sample: Which gas can you treat as ideal without much worry?
questionPlan.answer: Air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure
choices: Steam at 100 C and 101 kPa, just at its boiling point
Steam at 22 MPa, close to water's critical point
Air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure
questionPlan.why: Near boiling a gas condenses on small pressure rises; at very high pressure intermolecular forces matter.

lessons.title: The energy balance on a device
lessons.objective: Write the steady-flow energy balance for a turbine, pump, condenser, heat exchanger or valve, drop the terms that do not matter, and solve for the unknown work, heat or flow.

concepts.title: Enthalpy
concepts.summary: h = u + Pv: the energy a flowing fluid carries across the boundary, including the work of pushing it in.

concepts.title: Steady-flow energy balance
concepts.summary: Per unit mass: h_in + ke_in + pe_in + q = h_out + ke_out + pe_out + w.

concepts.title: Terms you can drop
concepts.summary: In a turbine the kinetic and potential energy changes are under 1 Btu/lbm against hundreds in enthalpy.

concepts.title: Delta h or cp delta T
concepts.summary: Q = m (h_out - h_in) works through a phase change; m cp delta T fails because temperature barely moves while steam condenses.

concepts.title: Throttling
concepts.summary: An ideal throttle valve has h_in = h_out, no work and no heat.

misconceptions: Use m cp delta T everywhere. During condensation delta T is tiny and the latent heat is missed.
Speed and height changes always matter. In a turbine they come to under 1 Btu/lbm against 243 of work.
A throttle valve removes heat or does work. The ideal valve keeps enthalpy constant.
A condenser destroys energy. The heat the steam gives up is the heat the cooling water gains.
sequence: List everything crossing a turbine: mass with its enthalpy, speed and height, heat, shaft work.
Introduce enthalpy as the bundle u + Pv and write the balance per unit mass.
Work the handbook's turbine and see how small the kinetic and potential terms are.
Pumps and valves: pump work is small, throttling keeps enthalpy constant.
Two-sided exchanger: balance steam against cooling water, and see why m cp delta T misses the latent heat.
Recap the habit: boundary, crossings, drop what is small, solve.
examples: Turbine: steam enters at h = 1,349 Btu/lbm and leaves at 1,100, with 5 Btu/lbm heat loss, 164 to 262 ft/s and a 6.5 ft drop. Work = 1,349 - 1,100 - 5 = 244 Btu/lbm; with the speed and height terms the handbook gets 243.17. The speed and height terms together shift the answer by 0.83 Btu/lbm.

Condenser: 2.0 x 10^6 kg/hr of steam enters at h = 2,574 kJ/kg and leaves as liquid at 125.8. Cooling water gains 75.6 to 104.9 kJ/kg. Flow = 2.0e6 x 2,448.2 / 29.3 = 1.67e8 kg/hr, about 84 kg of water per kg of steam.
Using m cp delta T on the 10 C of subcooling gives 4.18 x 10 = 42 kJ/kg, 1.7% of the real 2,448 kJ/kg.

figures.shows: A turbine control volume with arrows for h_in, h_out, shaft work and heat loss, and a bar chart beside it: enthalpy drop 249 Btu/lbm against kinetic plus potential change 0.83 Btu/lbm.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle 'include speed and height' and watch the work change by less than 1 Btu/lbm.

figures.shows: Condenser states: steam in (2,574), condensate out (125.8), cooling water in (75.6) and out (104.9), in kJ/kg.
figures.learnerAction: Compute each side's enthalpy change and the flow ratio.

questionPlan.sample: Steam enters a turbine at h = 1,349 Btu/lbm and leaves at 1,100 Btu/lbm. Heat loss is 5 Btu/lbm. Ignoring speed and height changes, what is the work per lbm?
questionPlan.answer: 244 Btu/lbm (accept 243 to 245)
questionPlan.why: w = h_in - h_out + q, with heat loss counted as negative heat in.

questionPlan.sample: Including speed and height changes shifts that turbine's work by less than 1 Btu/lbm. What should you conclude?
questionPlan.answer: They can go if the enthalpy drop is in the hundreds
choices: They must always be kept in a turbine's energy balance
They can go if the enthalpy drop is in the hundreds
They are zero for any turbine with a casing
questionPlan.why: They are small, not zero. Whether they matter depends on the size of the enthalpy change.

questionPlan.sample: 100 kg/s of steam enters a condenser at h = 2,574 kJ/kg and leaves as liquid at 125.8 kJ/kg. Cooling water enters at 75.6 and leaves at 104.9 kJ/kg. What cooling-water flow is needed?
questionPlan.why: Steam's enthalpy loss equals the water's enthalpy gain.

questionPlan.sample: A student finds the heat given up in a condenser as m cp delta T over the 10 C of subcooling and gets about 42 kJ per kg of steam. The enthalpies give 2,448 kJ/kg. What went wrong?
questionPlan.answer: It missed the latent heat released during condensation
choices: It missed the latent heat released during condensation
The specific heat of water was out by a factor of ten or so
Subcooling should be counted twice for two sides
questionPlan.why: cp delta T only covers the temperature change of the liquid.

questionPlan.sample: Refrigerant passes through a throttle valve and its pressure drops. Which quantity does the ideal analysis keep constant?
questionPlan.answer: Enthalpy
choices: Pressure
Enthalpy
Temperature
questionPlan.why: An ideal throttle is adiabatic with no work, so h_in = h_out. Pressure is what the valve changes; for real fluids temperature changes too.

lessons.title: Testing a claimed efficiency
lessons.objective: Compute the Carnot limit between two temperatures, use it to test a claimed efficiency, and say which limits come from the second law and which from materials and the environment.

concepts.title: The second law
concepts.summary: No cycle turns all its heat into work, and heat does not flow from cold to hot with no other effect; work can be turned into heat completely.

concepts.title: Carnot efficiency
concepts.summary: eta = 1 - Tc/Th with absolute temperatures; no engine between the same two reservoirs does better.

concepts.title: Practical limits
concepts.summary: The sink is the environment (about 60 F) and the source is capped by materials (about 1,500 F), giving 73.5%; real fossil plants reach about 40%.

misconceptions: Better engineering can approach 100%. The second law caps even a perfect machine.
Celsius or Fahrenheit values can go into the Carnot formula. They must be absolute.
Carnot efficiency is what a good engine achieves. Real examples reach about half of it (18% against 35%; about 40% against 73.5%).
Carnot efficiency falls as the source gets hotter. It rises; the source is limited by materials, not by the law.
sequence: Start with a datasheet claim: 38% from a 600 C source rejecting at 25 C. Possible or not?
State the second law the two historical ways, and the work-to-heat asymmetry.
Carnot's principle in three statements, then the formula with absolute temperatures.
Run the datasheet claim: limit 65.9%, claim is 58% of it.
See what real plants reach: the handbook's 18% against 35%, and about 40% against 73.5%.
Separate the limits: the law, the environment (sink) and materials (source).
examples: The handbook's inventor: 25 Btu of work from 100 Btu between 140 F and 0 F. Limit = 1 - 460/600 = 23.3%, so 25% is impossible.
A steam cycle at 18% from a 340 F source to a 60 F sink: limit 1 - 520/800 = 35%, so the real plant reaches 51% of its limit.
Practical ceiling: 1 - 520/1,960 = 73.5%; real fossil plants about 40% and nuclear about 31%.

figures.shows: Carnot efficiency against source temperature for a 300 K sink, with a second line at half the Carnot value for real plants.
figures.learnerAction: Drag a point along the source temperature and read both values.

figures.shows: A claims table: source, sink, claimed efficiency, Carnot limit, verdict.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in the limit and choose impossible, implausible or plausible for each row.

questionPlan.sample: A steam source is at 540 C and the condenser at 30 C. What is the Carnot efficiency, in percent? (K = C + 273.)
questionPlan.answer: 62.7 (accept 62 to 63)
questionPlan.why: Use absolute temperatures: 1 - 303/813.

questionPlan.sample: A datasheet says an engine converts 38% of the heat from a 600 C source into work while rejecting heat at 25 C. The Carnot limit is 65.9%. What is the fair verdict?
questionPlan.answer: Possible, at about 58% of the limit, as real plants show
choices: Possible, at about 58% of the limit, as real plants show
Impossible, since any engine loses over half its heat
Possible, since the Celsius figures give a limit of 95.8%
questionPlan.why: No law caps efficiency at one half; real plants reach roughly half of Carnot. The 95.8% comes from using Celsius, which is wrong.

questionPlan.sample: An inventor says an engine takes 100 kJ from a source at 450 K, rejects heat at 300 K and delivers 40 kJ of work. What is the verdict?
questionPlan.answer: Not possible: 40% is above the 33% Carnot limit
choices: Not possible: 40% is above the 33% Carnot limit
Possible, since 40% is well below the 100% mark
Possible, if the engine is insulated better
questionPlan.why: 1 - 300/450 = 33.3%. Insulation cannot beat the second law.

questionPlan.sample: Why do steam plants not simply run their boilers at 3,000 F?
questionPlan.answer: Boiler metals cannot survive it, which limits the source
choices: The second law rules out any source temperature that high
Boiler metals cannot survive it, which limits the source
Carnot efficiency drops as the source gets hotter
questionPlan.why: Carnot efficiency rises with source temperature. The limit is metallurgical, about 1,500 F.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each statement as set by the second law, the environment or materials: (1) no cycle turns all its heat into work, (2) heat is finally rejected to the earth at about 60 F, (3) boiler metals cap the source near 1,500 F, (4) no engine beats a reversible one between the same two temperatures.
questionPlan.answer: Second law: 1 and 4. Environment: 2. Materials: 3
choices: Second law
Environment
Materials
questionPlan.why: The law sets the form of the limit; temperatures come from surroundings and hardware.

historyNotes: The handbook dates Clausius's statement of the second law to 1850 and Sadi Carnot's principle to 1824.

lessons.title: Where real machines lose work
lessons.objective: Compute the isentropic efficiency of a turbine or pump from enthalpies, read an ideal and a real process on a T-s diagram, and name the cause of an irreversibility.

concepts.title: Entropy
concepts.summary: A property; for a reversible process delta S = Q / T. It cannot fall around a cycle and measures energy no longer available for work.

concepts.title: Isentropic process
concepts.summary: Reversible and adiabatic; a vertical line on a T-s diagram. A real expansion leans to the right.

concepts.title: Isentropic efficiency
concepts.summary: Turbine: actual work over ideal work. Pump or compressor: ideal work over actual work.

concepts.title: Causes of irreversibility
concepts.summary: Friction, unrestrained expansion, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, and mixing.

misconceptions: Adiabatic means isentropic. Isentropic needs the process to be reversible as well.
A real turbine destroys energy. The energy leaves in the exhaust, which ends at a higher enthalpy, so less work is taken out.
Pump efficiency is actual over ideal, like a turbine. It is ideal over actual, because a real pump needs more work.
Small turbines are as efficient as large ones. The handbook gives 60 to 80% for small and about 90% for large.
sequence: Draw an ideal expansion as a vertical T-s line and a real one leaning right; ask what the lean costs.
Entropy as Q/T, and heat rejected as sink temperature times entropy gained.
Turbine isentropic efficiency with enthalpies read from a Mollier example: 1,333 to 1,178 ideal.
Pump efficiency with the handbook's 75% case, and why the ratio is inverted.
Name the four causes of irreversibility and find each in a steam plant.
Judge plausibility: what does 73% mean for a large turbine?
examples: Superheated steam at 700 psia and 680 F expands isentropically to 140 psia: h falls from 1,333 to 1,178 Btu/lbm, ideal work 155 Btu/lbm. A real turbine ending at 1,220 has eta = 113/155 = 0.73.
At eta = 0.85 the same expansion gives 131.75 Btu/lbm of work and an exit enthalpy of 1,201.25.
Pump at 75% with ideal exit enthalpy 600 from 200 Btu/lbm: actual = 200 + 400/0.75 = 733.3.

figures.shows: A T-s diagram of one expansion: a vertical ideal line and a leaning real line, with the entropy gained shaded.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the exit point to the right and watch isentropic efficiency fall.

figures.shows: Four cases of irreversibility with a blank 'cause' column.
figures.learnerAction: Match each case to its cause.

questionPlan.sample: Steam enters a turbine at h = 1,333 Btu/lbm. An isentropic expansion would end at 1,178 Btu/lbm; the real turbine ends at 1,220. What is its isentropic efficiency?
questionPlan.why: Actual enthalpy drop over ideal enthalpy drop: 113/155.

questionPlan.sample: A report lists that 0.73 for the low-pressure turbine of a large utility plant. What is the fair reading?
questionPlan.answer: Low for a large turbine, which reaches about 0.90
choices: Low for a large turbine, which reaches about 0.90
Typical: all turbines sit close to 0.73
Impossible: a turbine's efficiency cannot fall below 0.80
questionPlan.why: The handbook gives 60 to 80% for small turbines and about 90% for large ones.

questionPlan.sample: A pump with 75% efficiency has an inlet enthalpy of 200 Btu/lbm. The ideal pump would deliver 600 Btu/lbm. What is the actual exit enthalpy?
questionPlan.answer: 733 Btu/lbm (accept 733 to 733.3)
questionPlan.why: The real pump needs ideal work divided by 0.75.

questionPlan.sample: On a T-s diagram a real turbine's expansion leans to the right of the vertical ideal line. What does the lean show?
questionPlan.answer: Entropy rose through friction, so less work came out
choices: Entropy rose through friction, so less work came out
Heat is added to the steam during expansion
The turbine ran faster than the designer intended it to
questionPlan.why: A vertical line is constant entropy. Leaning right means entropy gained.

questionPlan.sample: Sort each case by its cause of irreversibility: (1) steam rubbing past turbine blades, (2) steam through a partly open valve, (3) hot gas heating water across a 500 F gap, (4) cooler feedwater joining a hotter stream in an open heater.
questionPlan.answer: Friction: 1. Unrestrained expansion: 2. Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference: 3. Mixing: 4
choices: Friction
Unrestrained expansion
Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference
Mixing
questionPlan.why: The four causes the handbook lists.

lessons.title: Reading and improving a steam cycle
lessons.objective: Trace the Rankine cycle through pump, boiler, turbine and condenser, compute its efficiency from state enthalpies, and decide which change raises it and why.

concepts.title: The four processes
concepts.summary: Pump (liquid, small work), boiler (heat in at constant pressure), turbine (work out), condenser (heat out at constant pressure).

concepts.title: Thermal efficiency
concepts.summary: Net work over heat in: (w_turbine - w_pump) / (h3 - h2).

concepts.title: Average heat-input temperature
concepts.summary: Raising the average temperature at which heat enters, or lowering the temperature at which it leaves, raises efficiency.

concepts.title: Superheat, reheat, regeneration
concepts.summary: Superheat and reheat also dry the exhaust; regeneration preheats feedwater with bled steam.

misconceptions: The pump costs a large share of the turbine output. Pumping liquid takes about 1 to 3%.
The condenser's heat is a design flaw. The second law requires heat rejection; the plume over a plant is cooling-system vapour.
Higher boiler pressure always helps. It also makes the exhaust wetter, which erodes blades, so plants superheat and reheat.
Condenser subcooling is harmless. It means extra heat must be put back in the boiler.
sequence: Four devices in a loop and the four processes, with the states numbered.
Write the four balances from control volumes: q_in = h3 - h2, w_t = h3 - h4, w_p = h2 - h1, q_out = h4 - h1.
Work a cycle from enthalpies (167.2, 182.0, 3,400, 2,200 kJ/kg) to get 36.8%.
Place the result against real plants: 35 to 42% for a single steam cycle, 40% at 24.1 MPa, 42% at 31 MPa and 600 C.
Ask what raises efficiency: higher average heat-input temperature (superheat, reheat, regeneration) and a colder condenser.
Trace a plant with reheat from steam generator to steam generator.
examples: h1 = 167.2 kJ/kg (saturated liquid at 40 C, 7.37 kPa, from the table). Pump work 14.8, so h2 = 182.0. Turbine from h3 = 3,400 to h4 = 2,200 gives 1,200 kJ/kg. q_in = 3,218.0, q_out = 2,032.8, net work 1,185.2, efficiency 36.8%. Pump work is 1.2% of turbine work.
Summer cooling water raises the condenser temperature; the cold side of the cycle warms and efficiency falls.
The handbook's plant: saturated steam at 540 F to the high-pressure turbine, 82.5% quality at its exit, reheated to 440 F, condenser at 1 psia.

figures.shows: A T-s diagram of a Rankine cycle with the area for heat in and heat out shaded; toggles for superheat, reheat and a warmer condenser.
figures.learnerAction: Switch each change on and read how the shaded areas and the efficiency change.

figures.shows: State table: 1 condensate, 2 after pump, 3 turbine inlet, 4 turbine exit, with h in kJ/kg.
figures.learnerAction: Compute q_in, w_turbine, w_pump and efficiency.

questionPlan.sample: A steam cycle has h1 = 167.2 (condensate), h2 = 182.0 (after the pump), h3 = 3,400 (turbine inlet) and h4 = 2,200 kJ/kg (turbine exit). What is its thermal efficiency, in percent?
A student's cycle calculation gives pump work equal to 25% of the turbine work. What should you suspect?
questionPlan.answer: A data or arithmetic error: liquid pumping takes 1 to 3%
choices: A data or arithmetic error: liquid pumping takes 1 to 3%
Normal: pumps usually take about a quarter of the turbine output
A sign that the turbine is unusually efficient
questionPlan.why: Liquid is nearly incompressible, so pumping it takes little work.

questionPlan.sample: Besides raising the average temperature of heat addition, why is steam superheated before the turbine?
questionPlan.answer: It keeps the exhaust drier, sparing the last blades
choices: It shrinks the pump needed to feed the boiler
It keeps the exhaust drier, sparing the last blades
It lowers the pressure inside the condenser
questionPlan.why: Without superheat the exhaust is very wet and droplets pit the blades.

questionPlan.sample: In summer the cooling water warms and the condenser pressure rises. What happens to cycle efficiency, and why?
questionPlan.answer: It falls, because heat is rejected at a higher temperature
choices: It falls, because heat is rejected at a higher temperature
It rises, because warmer cooling water carries more heat away
It stays put, because the boiler fixes the efficiency
questionPlan.why: A warmer cold side narrows the temperature range the cycle works across.

questionPlan.sample: Put these steps of a steam plant with reheat in order, starting at the steam generator: (a) low-pressure turbine, (b) steam generator, (c) condenser, (d) high-pressure turbine, (e) condensate and feed pumps with feedwater heaters, (f) moisture separator and reheater.
questionPlan.answer: b, d, f, a, c, e
questionPlan.why: The steam is expanded, dried and reheated, expanded again, condensed, then pumped back.

historyNotes: The Rankine article says the reheat cycle was first introduced in the 1920s.

lessons.title: Gas turbines and the pressure ratio
lessons.objective: Compute the ideal Brayton efficiency from the pressure ratio, explain why real machines stop at pressure ratios of 11 to 16, and say when a recuperator pays.

concepts.title: Brayton cycle
concepts.summary: Compressor, combustor and turbine; the turbine drives the compressor and the rest of its work is the output.

concepts.title: Ideal efficiency
concepts.summary: eta = 1 - (P_in / P_out)^((gamma - 1)/gamma): it depends on the pressure ratio and gamma, not on the peak temperature.

concepts.title: Pressure-ratio limit
concepts.summary: A higher ratio makes the compressor outlet hotter, which leaves less temperature rise before the turbine's metal limit.

concepts.title: Recuperator
concepts.summary: A heat exchanger that preheats compressed air with exhaust; it only works when the pressure ratio is low.

misconceptions: A higher pressure ratio is always better. Compressor outlet temperature rises and the allowed fuel heat shrinks.
All the turbine's output goes to the generator. Part drives the compressor.
The ideal efficiency depends on turbine inlet temperature. The formula has only pressure ratio and gamma; inlet temperature changes the power per kg of air.
Ideal and real efficiencies agree. Simple-cycle machines in the pack sit near 41.5 to 43%.
sequence: Name the three components and follow air round the open cycle.
Give the ideal efficiency formula and compute a few pressure ratios with gamma = 1.4.
Ask why designers stop at 11 to 16: compressor outlet temperature, turbine metal limit.
Add the recuperator and the low-pressure-ratio condition.
Compare ideal with real simple-cycle efficiencies of 41.5 to 43%.
examples: gamma = 1.4: r_p = 8 gives 44.8%; 11 gives 49.6%; 12 gives 50.8%; 16 gives 54.7%; 30 gives 62.2%.
Open-circuit gas turbine firing temperatures run from 900 to 1,400 C; a quoted large turbine at 41.5% simple cycle.

figures.shows: Ideal Brayton efficiency against pressure ratio from 2 to 30 for gamma = 1.4, with the 11 to 16 band shaded.
figures.learnerAction: Move a marker along the curve and read the efficiency.

figures.shows: A T-s sketch of the Brayton cycle with a horizontal line at the turbine's temperature limit; the learner raises the pressure ratio and the heat-addition leg shortens.
figures.learnerAction: Raise the pressure ratio and watch the room under the limit shrink.

questionPlan.sample: What is the ideal Brayton efficiency, in percent, at a pressure ratio of 12 with gamma = 1.4?
A designer proposes a pressure ratio of 30 to gain efficiency. What is the main practical objection?
questionPlan.answer: Hot compressor air leaves little room under the metal limit
choices: The ideal efficiency starts to fall once the ratio passes 16
Carnot's theorem rules out ratios above about 16
Hot compressor air leaves little room under the metal limit
questionPlan.why: The ideal formula keeps rising with the ratio; the limit is the metal temperature.

questionPlan.sample: A catalogue gives an ideal 50.8% at a pressure ratio of 12 and a measured simple-cycle 41.5%. What best explains the gap?
questionPlan.answer: Compression and expansion are not isentropic, plus other losses
choices: Compression and expansion are not isentropic, plus other losses
The formula holds for closed cycles only, so is no guide
Air has a lower gamma than the ideal model assumes it has
questionPlan.why: Open cycles are analysed as closed ones; the gap is real irreversibility.

questionPlan.sample: A small engine runs at a low pressure ratio and its exhaust is still hotter than the compressed air. Would a recuperator help?
questionPlan.answer: Yes, the hot exhaust can preheat the compressed air
choices: Yes, the hot exhaust can preheat the compressed air
No, a recuperator only helps at high pressure ratios
No, a recuperator only works with a closed cycle
questionPlan.why: A recuperator needs the exhaust to be hotter than the compressed air, which happens at low pressure ratio.

lessons.title: Petrol and diesel engines
lessons.objective: Use the ideal Otto and Diesel efficiency formulas to compare the engines, explain why compression ratio is limited in one and not the other, and judge claims about turbochargers and superchargers.

concepts.title: Otto cycle
concepts.summary: Isentropic compression, constant-volume heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-volume rejection; eta = 1 - 1/r^(gamma-1).

concepts.title: Knock
concepts.summary: A petrol-air mixture that gets too hot during compression ignites early; this caps the compression ratio.

concepts.title: Diesel cycle
concepts.summary: Air is compressed and the fuel ignites by the heat of compression; heat is added at constant pressure, and efficiency also depends on the cut-off ratio.

concepts.title: Turbocharger and supercharger
concepts.summary: A turbocharger recovers exhaust energy; a crankshaft-driven supercharger raises power but not efficiency.

misconceptions: The Diesel cycle is more efficient than the Otto cycle at the same compression ratio. The ideal Otto cycle is.
Ideal formulas give real efficiency. They give upper bounds; real engines are significantly lower.
A supercharger makes an engine more efficient. It uses engine work to raise power.
Compression ratio can be raised freely. In a petrol engine knock stops it near 10:1.
sequence: Walk the four processes of the Otto cycle and the compression ratio.
Derive eta = 1 - r^(1-gamma) and compute values for r from 8 to 12.
Show the effect of gamma: 1.4 for air, about 1.3 for combustion products.
Explain knock and the 10:1 limit; contrast with diesel self-ignition.
Compare ideal Otto and ideal Diesel at the same r, then explain why real diesels win.
Judge a turbocharger and a supercharger claim.
examples: At r = 10 with gamma = 1.3 the ideal efficiency is 49.9%, so the choice of gamma moves the answer by ten points.
The pack's very large marine diesels burn 0.16 kg of fuel per kWh, the lowest of any single-cycle large engine.

figures.shows: Ideal Otto efficiency against compression ratio from 4 to 20 for gamma = 1.4 and 1.3, with a marker at the knock-limited 10:1.
figures.learnerAction: Move the ratio and read both curves.
figures.placement: Compression ratio and the knock limit

figures.shows: P-V sketches of the Otto and Diesel cycles side by side, heat addition marked as constant volume and constant pressure.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle the cut-off ratio on the Diesel sketch.

questionPlan.sample: What is the ideal Otto efficiency, in percent, at a compression ratio of 9 with gamma = 1.4?
questionPlan.answer: 58.5 (accept 58 to 59)

questionPlan.sample: Why is a petrol engine not built with a compression ratio of 20 to gain efficiency?
questionPlan.answer: The mixture would ignite on its own early: knock
choices: The ideal efficiency stops rising above about 12
Higher ratios need more fuel per power stroke
The mixture would ignite on its own early: knock
questionPlan.why: The formula keeps rising; autoignition is the limit.

questionPlan.sample: At the same compression ratio the ideal Otto cycle beats the ideal Diesel cycle, yet diesel engines are more efficient in practice. Why?
questionPlan.answer: They run at higher ratios, since self-ignition suits them
choices: The Diesel formula overstates what real diesels can reach
They run at higher ratios, since self-ignition suits them
Diesel fuel carries more energy per kilogram of fuel
questionPlan.why: Higher ratio, not a better cycle at equal ratio.

questionPlan.sample: A tuner fits a crankshaft-driven supercharger and says the engine is now more efficient. What is the fair response?
questionPlan.answer: It adds power, not efficiency, as it takes engine work
choices: It adds power, not efficiency, as it takes engine work
It raises efficiency, because more air lets more fuel burn
A supercharger and a turbocharger do the same thing
questionPlan.why: A turbocharger takes energy from the exhaust; the supercharger takes it from the crankshaft.

questionPlan.sample: At r = 10 the ideal efficiency is 60.2% with gamma = 1.4 and 49.9% with gamma = 1.3. What does that show about ideal-cycle figures?
questionPlan.answer: Ideal figures are upper bounds that depend on the gas model
choices: Ideal figures match what real engines achieve in everyday driving
Ideal figures are upper bounds that depend on the gas model
Gamma only matters for diesel engines, not for petrol
questionPlan.why: The pack also says the real thermal efficiency is significantly lower.

lessons.title: Stacking cycles and using the waste heat
lessons.objective: Combine the efficiencies of a gas-turbine topping cycle and a steam bottoming cycle, compare efficiencies stated on different fuel bases, and say what a combined heat and power figure does and does not tell you.

concepts.title: Topping and bottoming cycles
concepts.summary: A gas turbine's hot exhaust raises steam for a second engine, so the same fuel runs two cycles.

concepts.title: Stacked efficiency
concepts.summary: eta_total = eta_top + (1 - eta_top) x eta_bottom; the bottoming cycle works only on what the first one left.

concepts.title: HHV and LHV
concepts.summary: Efficiency quoted on the lower heating value reads higher than on the higher heating value; for methane the two differ by about 11%.

concepts.title: Combined heat and power
concepts.summary: A total that counts both electricity and useful heat is not an electrical efficiency.

misconceptions: Efficiencies add: 43% + 37% = 80%. The steam cycle only gets the 57% the gas turbine left.
LHV and HHV figures can be compared directly. They differ by about 11% for methane.
A CHP total of 90% means 90% electricity. It counts heat too.
A combined-cycle plant always runs at 60%. Peak steady-state is 55 to 59% on LHV, and start-up and part load cost efficiency.
sequence: Show why a gas turbine's exhaust is still hot (450 to 650 C) and what can use it.
Stack the two efficiencies correctly: 43% simple to 64% combined, and what the steam cycle must have done.
Explain why steam is the bottoming cycle: its lower entry temperature suits the exhaust.
Compare efficiency claims on different fuel bases with the 11% factor.
Look at CHP totals above 90% and ask what they hide.
Check part-load and start-up penalties.
examples: Gas turbine alone 43%, combined 64%: (0.64 - 0.43) / 0.57 = 37% of the exhaust heat was converted, inside the 35 to 42% range of a single steam plant.
A plant quoted at 60% on LHV is 0.60 x 50.00 / 55.50 = 54% on HHV, as the pack says of the Baglan Bay plant (nearly 60% LHV, 54% HHV).
A CHP plant: 35% electricity and 55% heat gives 90% total but still 35% electrical.

figures.shows: A stacked bar of fuel energy: gas turbine output 43%, steam cycle output 21%, losses 36% (64% combined), with a second bar for a 35% electric, 55% heat CHP plant.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the bottoming efficiency and watch the combined total.

figures.shows: Four plant claims with their basis (LHV or HHV) and a column for the comparable HHV value.
figures.learnerAction: Convert each to HHV.

questionPlan.sample: A gas turbine alone converts 43% of the fuel energy; with the steam cycle added the plant reaches 64%. What fraction of the turbine's leftover heat did the steam cycle convert, in percent?
questionPlan.answer: 37 (accept 36 to 38)

questionPlan.sample: Why is the combined efficiency not simply 43% + 37%?
questionPlan.answer: The steam cycle only gets the 57% left after the turbine
choices: Steam cycles lose about 20% of their output in the generator
Efficiencies only add when both cycles run on steam
The steam cycle only gets the 57% left after the turbine
questionPlan.why: The second engine works on the first one's exhaust, not on all the fuel.

questionPlan.sample: Plant A advertises 60% on a lower heating value basis. Plant B advertises 55% on a higher heating value basis. Which is more efficient on one basis?
questionPlan.answer: Plant B, since A is about 54% on the HHV basis
choices: Plant B, since A is about 54% on the HHV basis
Plant A, since 60% is clearly higher than 55%
They are equal, since the bases differ by one point
questionPlan.why: LHV over HHV is 55.50/50.00 for methane, so 60% LHV is 54% HHV.

questionPlan.sample: A CHP plant reports a 90% total: 35% electricity and 55% heat. A grid planner asks how much of the fuel becomes electricity. What is the answer?
questionPlan.answer: 35%, since the 90% also counts heat
choices: 90%, the figure on the report
35%, since the 90% also counts heat
55%, since heat is the larger share
questionPlan.why: A total efficiency counts heat that is lower-grade than electricity.

questionPlan.sample: Why is a steam cycle used to bottom a gas turbine, not the other way round?
questionPlan.answer: Steam cycles accept heat at lower temperatures
choices: Steam cycles accept heat at lower temperatures
Steam turbines are lighter and cheaper than gas turbines
Steam can reach 1,400 C, above gas turbines
questionPlan.why: Steam plant entry temperatures are low compared with gas turbine firing temperatures.

lessons.title: Moving heat with work
lessons.objective: Name the four components of a vapour-compression machine, compute COP for cooling and heating, and judge a quoted COP against the Carnot limit at the stated temperatures.

concepts.title: Vapour-compression cycle
concepts.summary: Compressor, condenser, expansion valve (throttle, constant enthalpy) and evaporator.

concepts.title: Coefficient of performance
concepts.summary: Useful heat moved over work in; COP_heating = COP_cooling + 1; a resistance heater has COP 1.

concepts.title: Carnot COP
concepts.summary: COP_heating = T_H / (T_H - T_C) with absolute temperatures; real machines reach a fraction of it.

concepts.title: Temperature lift
concepts.summary: COP falls as the gap between source and delivery temperature widens.

misconceptions: COP above 1 breaks energy conservation. The machine moves heat that already exists; the first law balances.
COP_heating equals COP_cooling. It is larger by exactly 1.
A machine has one COP. It depends on the two temperatures.
Celsius values can go into the Carnot COP. They must be absolute.
sequence: Follow refrigerant round the four components; the throttle keeps enthalpy constant.
Define COP and show why heating COP exceeds cooling COP by one.
Derive the Carnot limit and compute 8.8 for 35 C from 0 C.
Read the real COP table against the Carnot rows.
Compare resistance heating (COP 1) and a heat pump (3 to 5 in mild conditions).
Show how delivery temperature and source temperature move the COP.
examples: Ground-source test conditions 308 K and 273 K: Carnot heating COP 8.8, cooling 7.8; best test results about 4.5; seasonal heating COP 3.5 or less.
A 10 K lift (270 K to 280 K) gives Carnot COP 28; a 30 K lift (to 300 K) gives 10.
Real air-source unit at 0 C air: COP 3.8 delivering 35 C, 2.2 delivering 55 C; at -20 C air: 2.2 delivering 35 C.

figures.shows: COP against delivery temperature (35 to 85 C) with the Carnot line for 0 C air and the real air-source line below it.
figures.learnerAction: Pick a source temperature and read the gap between real and Carnot.

figures.shows: A four-box vapour-compression loop with the heat flows Q_C and Q_H and the work W labelled.
figures.learnerAction: Tap a flow to see Q_H = Q_C + W.

questionPlan.sample: A ground-source heat pump delivers heat at 35 C from a source at 0 C. What is the Carnot limit on its heating COP? (K = C + 273.)
questionPlan.answer: 8.8 (accept 8.7 to 8.9)

questionPlan.sample: A brochure gives a COP of 9.5 for an air-source unit that delivers 35 C from 0 C air. What is the right reaction?
questionPlan.answer: Impossible: it is above the Carnot limit of 8.8
choices: Plausible, since COP values above 1 are normal
Impossible: it is above the Carnot limit of 8.8
Plausible if the compressor is efficient enough
questionPlan.why: No compressor efficiency gets past the Carnot COP.

questionPlan.sample: Ground-source COPs from the table: 0 C water source, 5.0 delivering 35 C and 2.9 delivering 55 C; 10 C ground source, 7.2 delivering 35 C and 3.7 delivering 55 C. A system delivers 55 C from 0 C water (COP 2.9). Which change raises its COP more?
questionPlan.answer: Delivering at 35 C instead, e.g. underfloor heating
choices: Moving to a 10 C ground source, still delivering at 55 C
Delivering at 35 C instead, e.g. underfloor heating
Neither; COP does not depend on temperatures
questionPlan.why: 35 C delivery gives 5.0, a gain of 2.1; the warmer source gives 3.7, a gain of 0.8.

questionPlan.sample: A heat pump draws 3.0 kW of heat from outdoor air using 1.0 kW of electricity. What is its heating COP?
questionPlan.why: Heat delivered is 3.0 + 1.0 = 4.0 kW, not 3.0.

questionPlan.sample: An air-source unit has COP 3.8 delivering 35 C from 0 C air and 2.2 from -20 C air. Why does it fall?
questionPlan.answer: The lift grows; the Carnot limit falls from 8.8 to 5.6
choices: Cold air carries less energy, so the compressor stalls
Heating COP always drops by one in cold weather
The lift grows; the Carnot limit falls from 8.8 to 5.6
questionPlan.why: Carnot COP = T_H / (T_H - T_C): a bigger gap lowers it.

lessons.title: Thermal resistance in series
lessons.objective: Build a series resistance network for a wall or pipe from conduction layers and convection films, find which resistance controls the heat flow, and decide whether more insulation helps.

concepts.title: Series resistance
concepts.summary: Heat flux = temperature difference over the sum of the layer resistances, each thickness / k.

concepts.title: Convection film
concepts.summary: Q = h A delta T; the film is one more resistance, 1/h; turbulent flow has higher h.

concepts.title: Dominant resistance
concepts.summary: The largest resistance sets the heat flow and takes most of the temperature drop.

concepts.title: Critical radius
concepts.summary: On a small cylinder, insulation below r = k/h raises heat loss.

misconceptions: Thicker insulation always cuts heat loss. On a very small cylinder it can raise it until the critical radius.
A good conductor next to the insulation matters. Its resistance is negligible beside the insulation's.
Every layer has the same temperature drop. The drop is proportional to the layer's resistance.
The air film can be ignored always. It is tiny next to insulation, but for an uninsulated surface it is the whole resistance.
sequence: Start with the heat flux through a three-layer wall and ask which layer to thicken.
Define resistance as thickness over k and add in series by analogy with electrical resistors.
Work the handbook's copper, asbestos and fibreglass wall: 7.79 total, 64.2 Btu/hr-ft2.
Add convection: Q = hA delta T, an uninsulated steam line, and the film as a resistance.
Move to a pipe: log-mean area, and a 12 in. pipe with 3 in. of insulation.
Critical radius k/h for a small wire or tube.
examples: Wall: copper 1 in. (k 240), asbestos 1/8 in. (0.048), fibreglass 2 in. (0.022); R = 0.000347, 0.2170, 7.5758 hr-ft2-F/Btu; total 7.793; 500 F gives 64.2 Btu/hr-ft2. Fibreglass is 97% of the resistance.
Uninsulated 22 ft steam line, 18 in. OD, surface 280 F, room 72 F, h = 18: Q = 3.88 x 10^5 Btu/hr.
Pipe wall k 12.5, 10 in. ID, 12 in. OD, 3 in. of asbestos (k 0.14), 550 F to 100 F: 971 Btu/hr per foot; the insulation holds 99.5% of the resistance.

figures.shows: A row of resistance bars for the three wall layers, each width proportional to R, with sliders for each thickness.
figures.learnerAction: Change a thickness and watch the total and the heat flux.

figures.shows: Heat loss from a small cylinder against insulation outer radius, rising to a peak near the critical radius, then falling.
figures.learnerAction: Move the radius and read the loss.

questionPlan.sample: A wall has resistances 0.000347, 0.2170 and 7.5758 hr-ft2-F/Btu in series and a 500 F difference across it. What is the heat flux in Btu/hr-ft2?
questionPlan.answer: 64.2 (accept 64 to 64.4)

questionPlan.sample: In that wall, which change cuts the heat loss most?
questionPlan.answer: The fibreglass, which holds 97% of the resistance
choices: The fibreglass, which holds 97% of the resistance
The copper plate, which the heat meets first
The asbestos layer, which is thinnest of the three
questionPlan.why: Doubling copper changes the total by about 0.005%.

questionPlan.sample: A 12 in. steel pipe (k 12.5) has 3 in. of insulation (k 0.14). Where does most of the temperature drop occur?
questionPlan.answer: Across the insulation, which has about 99% of it
choices: Across the steel wall, because metal is so dense
Equally across both, as the same heat flows
Across the insulation, which has about 99% of it

questionPlan.sample: Insulation with k = 0.14 Btu/hr-ft-F goes on a thin hot wire in air with h = 18 Btu/hr-ft2-F. At what outer radius, in inches, does adding insulation start to cut heat loss?
A flat wall has 1 in. of insulation (k 0.8) and an outside air film with h = 950. Why can the film be ignored?
questionPlan.answer: Its resistance, about 0.001, is tiny next to 0.104
choices: Films never matter in any heat transfer problem at all
Its resistance, about 0.001, is tiny next to 0.104
Still air carries no heat by convection at all

lessons.title: Heat exchangers
lessons.objective: Choose between parallel flow and counter-flow, compute the log mean temperature difference, and see how film coefficients set the overall coefficient U.

concepts.title: Parallel flow and counter-flow
concepts.summary: Counter-flow gives a more even temperature difference; the cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid's outlet.

concepts.title: Log mean temperature difference
concepts.summary: (delta T2 - delta T1) / ln(delta T2 / delta T1) from the temperature differences at the two ends.

concepts.title: Overall coefficient
concepts.summary: U = 1 / (1/h1 + thickness/k + 1/h2) for a thin wall; Q = U A LMTD.

concepts.title: The smaller h dominates
concepts.summary: Improving the poorer film pays more than improving the better one.

misconceptions: Parallel flow transfers as much heat for the same size. It needs about 15% more area in the handbook's case.
The arithmetic mean difference is always fine. The log mean is the right average along the exchanger.
In parallel flow the cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid. It cannot.
Improving either film helps equally. The smaller h limits U.
sequence: Sketch temperatures along parallel and counter-flow exchangers.
State the advantages and disadvantages of each as the handbook lists them.
Define the log mean temperature difference and compute 232 F for the handbook case.
Compute the same duty in parallel flow (201 F) and the area ratio.
Build U from two films and a thin wall: 827.6 Btu/hr-ft2-F for the condenser tube.
Ask which film to improve.
examples: Counter-flow: cold 120 to 310 F, hot 500 to 400 F: end differences 280 and 190; LMTD = 90 / ln(280/190) = 232 F.
Same temperatures in parallel flow: differences 380 and 90; LMTD = 290 / ln(380/90) = 201 F; for equal U and duty the area is 232/201 = 1.15 times as large.
Condenser tube: h inside 2,000, h outside 1,500, copper k 200, wall 0.1 in.: U = 827.6; per foot of 0.75 in. tube Q = 37,700 Btu/hr.
Doubling the outside film (1,500 to 3,000) gives U = 1,143; doubling the inside film gives 1,043.

figures.shows: Temperature against length along an exchanger for counter-flow and parallel flow, with the end differences marked.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the arrangement and read the end differences.

figures.shows: Terminal temperatures and film coefficients for the condenser tube.
figures.learnerAction: Compute U and the effect of doubling each film.

questionPlan.sample: A counter-flow exchanger heats a fluid from 120 F to 310 F with a hot fluid entering at 500 F and leaving at 400 F. What is the log mean temperature difference, in F?
questionPlan.answer: 232 (accept 231 to 233)

questionPlan.sample: Which arrangement can heat the cold fluid to a temperature above the hot fluid's outlet temperature?
questionPlan.answer: Counter-flow only
choices: Parallel flow only
Counter-flow only
Either, if the flow is fast enough
questionPlan.why: In parallel flow the cold fluid's outlet never exceeds the lowest hot-fluid temperature.

questionPlan.sample: For the same four terminal temperatures run in parallel flow, the log mean difference is 201 F against 232 F in counter-flow. How many times as much area does the parallel exchanger need for the same duty and U?
questionPlan.why: Q = U A LMTD, so area scales as 1/LMTD.

questionPlan.sample: A condenser tube has an inner film h = 2,000 and an outer film h = 1,500, with a thin copper wall. Which single doubling raises U more?
questionPlan.answer: Doubling the outer film, 1,500 to 3,000
choices: Doubling the inner film, 2,000 to 4,000
Doubling the outer film, 1,500 to 3,000
Both raise U by the same amount
questionPlan.why: U goes from 828 to 1,143 with the outer film and to 1,043 with the inner film.

questionPlan.sample: When is a parallel-flow design the right choice?
questionPlan.answer: When both fluids should end at nearly one temperature
choices: When the cold fluid must end as hot as possible
When thermal stress on the tubes must be as small as possible
When both fluids should end at nearly one temperature
questionPlan.why: The handbook gives that as parallel flow's advantage; counter-flow wins on the other two.

lessons.title: Following the fuel through a power station
lessons.objective: Convert a heat rate to an efficiency, estimate the heat a plant does not turn into electricity, and tell from the figures which stated efficiencies are implausible.

concepts.title: Heat rate
concepts.summary: Fuel energy in Btu per net kWh generated; efficiency = 3,412 / heat rate.

concepts.title: Rejected heat
concepts.summary: Fuel energy minus electricity: for the average coal plant about 68% of the fuel energy.

concepts.title: Fleet average against new-build
concepts.summary: EIA's yearly averages cover the whole running fleet, not the best new plant.

concepts.title: Plausibility check
concepts.summary: A stated efficiency must sit below the Carnot-based ceiling and near the range for that plant type.

misconceptions: A lower heat rate means a worse plant. It means less fuel per kWh, which is better.
The plume over a power station is the steam cycle's exhaust. It is cooling-system vapour.
Rejected heat is a design failure. The second law requires it.
Fleet averages describe new plants. Averages include old units.
sequence: Define heat rate and convert it with 3,412 Btu/kWh.
Read the 2025 averages: coal 10,647, petroleum 10,969, natural gas 7,781, nuclear 10,443 Btu/kWh.
Estimate rejected heat per kWh of electricity and tie it back to the condenser.
Read the ten-year trend: gas down, coal slightly up.
Set the averages beside the pack's expected ranges: 35 to 42% for a single steam plant, about 62% best combined cycle.
Test press-release claims for plausibility.
examples: Coal 10,647: 3,412 / 10,647 = 32.0%; rejected 7,235 Btu per kWh, 68% of the fuel. Gas 7,781: 43.9%, rejected 56%. Nuclear 10,443: 32.7%.
Heat rate 6,000 Btu/kWh is 56.9%: a steam plant cannot do that, a best combined cycle approaches 62%.

figures.shows: A fuel-to-electricity bar for coal, gas and nuclear with the electricity share (3,412 Btu) and the rest drawn to scale from 10,647, 7,781 and 10,443 Btu.
figures.learnerAction: Tap a bar to read the share rejected.

figures.shows: Average heat rate by fuel from 2015 to 2025.
figures.learnerAction: Pick a fuel to read the trend.

questionPlan.sample: In 2025 the average US coal plant had a heat rate of 10,647 Btu/kWh. What efficiency is that, in percent?
The average natural gas plant in 2025 used 7,781 Btu of fuel per kWh. How many Btu of fuel energy per kWh did not leave as electricity?
Which statement do EIA's 2015 and 2025 averages support?
questionPlan.answer: Gas heat rate fell slightly; coal's rose slightly
choices: Coal plants became much more efficient over the decade
All four fuels improved their heat rate by 5% or more
Gas heat rate fell slightly; coal's rose slightly
questionPlan.why: A rising heat rate is a falling efficiency.

questionPlan.sample: A press release says a new coal-fired steam station reaches a heat rate of 6,000 Btu/kWh. What should an engineer say?
questionPlan.answer: 57% efficiency: beyond a steam cycle's 35 to 42%
choices: Plausible, since coal is an energy-dense fuel
57% efficiency: beyond a steam cycle's 35 to 42%
17% efficiency, which would be very poor for coal

questionPlan.sample: The white plume above a power station is best described as:
questionPlan.answer: Vapour from the cooling system, not the steam loop
choices: Vapour from the cooling system, not the steam loop
Exhaust steam coming straight off the turbine
Smoke and flue gases from the burning of the fuel
questionPlan.why: The steam loop is closed; the plume comes from the cooling water.

lessons.title: Judging energy claims
lessons.objective: Turn nameplate capacity into delivered energy with capacity factors, and compare heating options by the fuel they burn, using COP and plant heat rate.

concepts.title: Capacity factor
concepts.summary: Energy a unit actually produced over what it would make at full power for the whole period; a measure of use, not of conversion efficiency.

concepts.title: Nameplate to energy
concepts.summary: Annual energy = capacity x 8,760 h x capacity factor.

concepts.title: Primary energy for heat
concepts.summary: Fuel per kWh of heat = (heat rate / 3,412) / COP for a heat pump, or 1 / efficiency for a boiler.

concepts.title: Grid dependence
concepts.summary: Whether a heat pump cuts emissions depends on the grid as well as on its COP.

misconceptions: Capacity factor is an efficiency. It is a measure of how much a plant runs.
A low capacity factor marks a bad plant. Gas turbines in 2025 ran at 13.6% by design as peaking units.
1 MW of solar equals 1 MW of nuclear. In 2025 PV ran at 24.0% and nuclear at 91.1%.
A heat pump always beats a gas boiler on fuel. It depends on COP and on the grid's heat rate.
sequence: Define capacity factor and read the 2025 table: nuclear 91.1%, combined cycle 58.7%, coal 48.8%, wind 33.8%, PV 24.0%, gas turbine 13.6%.
Turn nameplate into annual energy and into equivalent capacity.
Count fuel per kWh of heat for resistance heating, a boiler and a heat pump on a gas-heavy grid.
Find the break-even COP against a 90% boiler.
Read the emissions table for different grids.
Test claims against the limits met earlier (Carnot COP, plausible efficiency).
examples: 100 MW of nuclear at 91.1% makes as much energy as 91.1/24.0 = 3.8 times as many MW of PV, 380 MW; or 2.7 times as many MW of wind.
Fuel per kWh of heat on a grid at 7,781 Btu/kWh: resistance 2.28 kWh; heat pump at COP 3, 0.76; gas boiler at 90%, 1.11. The break-even COP is 2.28 / 1.11 = 2.05.
Emissions: heat pump on lignite at COP 3, 407 gCO2/kWh of heat; gas boiler 223; heat pump on wind 3; on the global mix 109.
DOE says air-source heat pumps cut electricity use by 50% against baseboard heaters, which fits a seasonal COP near 2.

figures.shows: Capacity factors for 2025 by technology with a column for annual energy of a 100 MW unit.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in the energy and the equivalent nuclear capacity.

figures.shows: Fuel per kWh of heat against heat pump COP (1 to 5) on three grids (gas average, coal average, nothing burned) with a horizontal line at the 90% boiler's 1.11.
figures.learnerAction: Move the COP and see where each grid crosses the boiler line.

questionPlan.sample: Using 2025 capacity factors, nuclear 91.1% and solar photovoltaic 24.0%, how many MW of solar capacity make as much annual energy as 100 MW of nuclear?
questionPlan.answer: 380 (accept 370 to 390)

questionPlan.sample: Gas combined-cycle plants ran at 58.7% in 2025 and gas turbines at 13.6%. A commentator says the gas turbines are inefficient. What is the fair reading?
questionPlan.answer: It shows how much the plant runs, not its efficiency
choices: It shows how much the plant runs, not its efficiency
The commentator is right: 13.6% is the efficiency figure
The turbines are faulty, since all plants reach 50%
questionPlan.why: The definition is energy produced over energy at continuous full power.

questionPlan.sample: On a grid supplied by gas plants with a heat rate of 7,781 Btu/kWh, what heat pump COP burns the same fuel per kWh of heat as a 90% efficient gas boiler? (Ignore grid losses.)
questionPlan.answer: 2.05 (accept 2.0 to 2.1)
questionPlan.why: Fuel per kWh heat: heat pump 2.28 / COP, boiler 1.11.

questionPlan.sample: On a lignite-fired grid a heat pump at COP 3 emits 407 gCO2 per kWh of heat, against 223 for a high-efficiency gas boiler. What does that show?
questionPlan.answer: The outcome depends on the grid as well as the COP
choices: Heat pumps always emit more than gas boilers
The COP figure for the lignite case must be mistaken
The outcome depends on the grid as well as the COP
questionPlan.why: On a wind grid the same heat pump emits 3 g.

questionPlan.sample: A tender claims a heat pump with COP 6 delivering 35 C from -20 C air. The Carnot limit for those conditions is 5.6 and the best real unit in the table reaches 2.2. What is the verdict?
questionPlan.answer: Impossible: 6 is above the Carnot limit of 5.6
choices: Impossible: 6 is above the Carnot limit of 5.6
Plausible: modern compressors can reach 6
Possible but optimistic, as 6 is close to the 5.6 limit
questionPlan.why: Above the Carnot limit is not optimistic, it is impossible.

courseCheck: A mixed check across the course. Classify the system and boundary for a pump, a turbine and a whole loop. Read a state from the saturation table and find its quality. Balance a turbine and a condenser from enthalpies. Test three efficiency claims against the Carnot limit. Compute an isentropic efficiency and a Rankine cycle efficiency from states. Compare ideal Brayton and Otto values with real figures. Stack a combined cycle and convert LHV to HHV. Check a COP against the Carnot COP. Find the dominant resistance in a wall and a pipe. Compute an LMTD. Convert a heat rate to efficiency, then use capacity factors and COP to compare energy options and spot the one figure in a set that is implausible.
platformNeeds: A steam-table lookup figure: choose T or P, see saturation values, hf, hfg and the region verdict. Fallback: the `table` figure with the pack's saturation rows (pack/wp-water-saturation-table.txt).
A T-s diagram explorer for a Rankine cycle with superheat, reheat and condenser sliders and a live efficiency. Fallback: `svg_figure` with three fixed variants the learner switches between.
A series-resistance bar figure with thickness sliders. Fallback: `svg_figure` with two fixed settings.
A to-scale energy flow bar (fuel, electricity, rejected heat). Fallback: `svg_figure`.
unverified: The pack has no entropy values and no superheated-steam table. Cycle questions give the state enthalpies in the prompt; they are illustrative and labelled as such (only h1 = 167.2 kJ/kg at 40 C comes from the pack's table).
Gamma = 1.4 for air comes from the Otto cycle page; no specific heats of gases are in the pack.
The specific volume of liquid water is not in the pack, so pump work is taken as a stated figure (1 to 3% of turbine work).

No real petrol or diesel engine efficiency is in the pack; only ideal values and the 0.16 kg/kWh marine diesel figure, which cannot be turned into an efficiency without a fuel heating value that the pack does not give.
The pack does not say whether EIA heat rates use higher or lower heating value, or what share of the rejected heat goes to the condenser against the stack.
Grid transmission and distribution losses are not in the pack; the heating-option comparison ignores them and must say so.

DOE handbook examples have small errors: Example 5 of the first law chapter gives 4,007 hp where 1.0e7 Btu/hr at 2,545 Btu/hr per hp is 3,929 hp; the quality example labels vg where vfg is meant. Neither is used.
The handbooks date from 1992 and mix English units; EIA data are for 2015 to 2025. Say which year each figure comes from.
The pack's saturation table gives h at 40 C as hf + hfg = 2,572.1 kJ/kg; the handbook uses 2,574 kJ/kg. Use each in its own case, not together.
NIST WebBook steam properties were not used: NIST says its Standard Reference Data may not be reproduced without permission.
